lesson.title: Twisted Pair Cable: Fighting Interference with Geometry
lesson.summary: Twisted pair cable defeats electromagnetic interference not with shielding but with a simple geometric trick, twisting two wires around each other so that stray noise affects both wires almost equally and cancels out at the receiver.
lesson.body:
The physical layer is where bits meet an actual physical medium, and twisted pair cable is one of the most common such media in real networks, from telephone wiring to the Ethernet cable running into most desktop computers. Structurally, it is nothing more exotic than two insulated copper wires twisted around each other along the cable's length, rather than run in parallel side by side. That twisting is not cosmetic; it is the entire mechanism that makes the cable usable in an electrically noisy environment.

Any external source of electromagnetic interference, a nearby power line, a fluorescent light ballast, another cable bundled alongside it, induces unwanted voltage onto exposed wires. If two wires ran perfectly parallel, one wire would sit slightly closer to the interference source than the other, so the induced noise would be different on each. But networking equipment reads twisted pair signals differentially, taking the voltage difference between the two wires as the actual signal rather than either wire's absolute voltage. Because the wires are twisted, each one spends roughly equal time closer to and farther from any external interference source along the cable's length, so the interference induces nearly identical noise voltage on both wires. When the receiver subtracts one wire's voltage from the other's, that shared, nearly identical noise largely cancels out, while the differential signal itself, which was deliberately driven with opposite polarity on the two wires, survives the subtraction intact.

Real twisted pair cables carrying multiple pairs, like the four pair cable behind most Ethernet jacks, apply this trick with a further refinement: each pair is twisted at a slightly different rate, a different number of twists per unit length, than its neighbors within the same cable jacket. This staggering reduces crosstalk, interference that one pair induces onto an adjacent pair, since pairs with mismatched twist rates align and misalign with each other constantly rather than staying in a fixed relationship that would let interference build up consistently.

Twisted pair comes in two broad varieties: unshielded twisted pair (UTP), which relies on twisting alone and dominates ordinary office and home Ethernet wiring, and shielded twisted pair (STP), which adds a metallic shield around the pairs for extra protection in electrically noisy environments, at higher cost and reduced flexibility. Cable categories such as Cat5e, Cat6, and Cat6a describe UTP cables built to progressively tighter manufacturing tolerances and tested to support progressively higher frequencies and thus higher data rates; a Cat5e cable, for example, is specified to reliably support 1000BASE-T Gigabit Ethernet over the standard 100 meter run using all four pairs simultaneously, something earlier, looser cable specifications could not guarantee.
